title: Jetpack Compose Fundamentals
summary: Compose renders UI as a function of state, re-running only what changed. Learn composables, recomposition, and state hoisting before the classic recomposition-skipping bugs bite you.

slides.markdown:
The classic Android View system is imperative: you call `textView.setText(...)` and mutate a live object tree by hand, and it's on you to keep every view in sync with whatever changed. **Jetpack Compose** flips that: you describe what the UI should look like *given the current state*, and Compose figures out what actually needs to be redrawn when that state changes.

The mental model shift is the whole topic: a composable function isn't called once to build a view — it's re-run (recomposed) whenever the state it reads changes, and Compose is smart enough to re-run only the composables that actually depend on what changed, not the whole tree. Getting this model right (and knowing exactly what breaks it) is the difference between a Compose UI that's fast by default and one that quietly re-renders everything on every keystroke.

slides.subTitle: UI as a function of state
slides.markdown:
A composable is a regular Kotlin function marked `@Composable` that describes a piece of UI by calling other composables — there's no view object you construct and hold onto; the function's *output*, given its current inputs, is the UI. Call the same composable with the same state twice and you get the same UI, the same way calling a pure function with the same arguments gives the same result.

This is the core conceptual break from the View system: instead of `button.setEnabled(isValid)` mutating an existing object, you write `Button(enabled = isValid) { ... }` as a description that's recomputed whenever `isValid` changes. There's no explicit "update the button" step to remember or forget to call — the description is simply re-evaluated, and Compose diffs the result against what's currently on screen.

The practical payoff: entire classes of bugs from the View system — a view left stale because an update call was missed, two pieces of code disagreeing about a view's current state — become structurally impossible, because there's no mutable view object to disagree about in the first place.

slides.sectionTitle: How recomposition re-runs only the affected composables
slides.markdown:
When a piece of state read by a composable changes, Compose doesn't re-run the whole UI tree from the root — it re-runs only the composables that actually **read** that specific piece of state, a mechanism called **smart recomposition**. A parent composable that merely contains a child reading the changed state, without reading it itself, is skipped entirely; only the child re-executes.

This works because Compose tracks reads of observable state (via `State<T>`, backed by `mutableStateOf`) at a fine granularity during composition, building a dependency graph between state and the composables that read it, rather than treating the whole tree as one unit that either re-runs or doesn't.

The consequence that matters day to day: a large screen with many independent widgets, each reading its own small piece of state, recomposes cheaply — only the one widget whose state changed re-runs. The same screen structured so every widget reads one shared top-level state object recomposes the *entire* screen on any change to any part of that object, because Compose can only skip what it can prove didn't need to change.

slides.subTitle: Lifting state up to make composables reusable

slides.markdown:
| | `remember` | `rememberSaveable` |
|---|---|---|
| **Survives recomposition** | Yes | Yes |
| **Survives a configuration change (rotation)** | No | Yes |
| **Survives process death** | No | Yes (backed by the same Bundle mechanism as View-system state saving) |
| **What it holds** | Any object | Primitives/Parcelable-friendly types by default; custom types need a Saver |

`remember` alone caches a value across recompositions within the *same* composition — it survives the UI re-rendering because state changed, but not the composable being torn down and rebuilt entirely, which is exactly what a rotation does. `rememberSaveable` layers the same Bundle-based save/restore mechanism the View system uses on top of `remember`, so the value survives both rotation and, if the data is small enough for a Bundle, process death.

The rule of thumb mirrors the Activity-level `ViewModel`-vs-`onSaveInstanceState` choice: use plain `remember` for transient UI state that's fine to reset on rotation (a temporary animation flag), and `rememberSaveable` for small state a user would notice disappearing (a text field's current input, a selected tab).

slides.subTitle: LaunchedEffect and DisposableEffect, and when to use each
slides.markdown:
A composable function is meant to be a pure description of UI — anything with a real side effect (starting a coroutine, subscribing to a callback API, logging an event) has to be explicitly scoped through a side-effect API, or it re-runs uncontrollably every single recomposition, which for something like starting a network request means firing it again and again as the UI merely redraws.

`LaunchedEffect(key)` runs a coroutine when the composable first enters composition, and re-runs it only if `key` changes — the standard tool for a one-shot or key-driven async operation (fetching data for a specific ID) tied to how long the composable is present. `DisposableEffect(key)` is for anything that needs explicit cleanup — subscribing to a callback-based API, a broadcast receiver, a listener — returning an `onDispose` block that Compose guarantees to call when the composable leaves composition or the key changes, which is where you unsubscribe.

The key parameter in both is what ties the effect's lifetime to something meaningful — passing a constant key means "run once for as long as this composable exists," while passing a value that changes (like a screen's item ID) means "restart the effect whenever that specific thing changes," not on every unrelated recomposition.

slides.sectionTitle: Jetpack Compose vs the classic View/XML system
slides.markdown:
| | View/XML | Compose |
|---|---|---|
| **UI definition** | XML layout + imperative Kotlin/Java to mutate views | Kotlin functions describing UI declaratively |
| **Update model** | You manually call setters to reflect new state | Recomposition automatically re-runs affected code on state change |
| **Reusability** | Custom View subclasses, somewhat heavyweight | Composable functions — as lightweight as any function |
| **Interop** | N/A | Full two-way interop with existing Views via adapters |

Compose isn't a from-scratch rewrite requirement — it interoperates with the View system in both directions, which is why most production migrations are incremental, converting screen by screen rather than as one large rewrite. The genuine trade-off, not just a preference: Compose's declarative model eliminates a whole category of manual-sync bugs, but it introduces its own new failure mode — a composable reading more state than it needs and recomposing (and potentially doing expensive work) far more often than necessary, which the next two slides cover directly.

slides.sectionTitle: Reading mutable state in a way that skips recomposition
slides.markdown:
A composable reads a plain `var` (not wrapped in `mutableStateOf` or an equivalent observable holder) and expects the UI to update when it changes. It doesn't — Compose's recomposition mechanism only knows to re-run a composable when it reads *observable* state through the `State<T>` snapshot system; a plain Kotlin `var` gives Compose nothing to subscribe to, so the value can change all it wants and the UI simply never notices.

This is confusing precisely because the code looks correct and even compiles cleanly — the mutation happens, the variable's value genuinely changes, and yet the screen appears frozen, which reads to a newcomer like a Compose bug rather than a fundamental misunderstanding of what makes something observable.

The fix is always wrapping UI-driving mutable state in an observable holder — `mutableStateOf`, a `StateFlow` collected with `collectAsState()`, or an equivalent — never a bare `var` outside of that system if a composable needs to react to its changes. The underlying rule: Compose reacts to *reads of observable state*, not to "the value changed" in any general sense.

slides.sectionTitle: Doing expensive work directly inside a composable body
slides.markdown:
A composable function calls into an expensive computation — filtering a large list, formatting a date, parsing something — directly in its body, with no memoization. Because that composable can recompose many times (every keystroke in a search field, every scroll event feeding it new data), the expensive work re-runs on every single recomposition, not once, turning what looks like a cheap function call into a real performance problem as the UI scales.

This is a natural mistake coming from the View system's mental model, where a function typically runs once when a view is built — in Compose, a composable body is expected to run *repeatedly*, and treating it like a one-time initialization block is the root of the bug.

The fix is `remember { expensiveComputation() }` (or, more precisely, `remember(keysThatShouldTriggerRecompute) { ... }`), which caches the result across recompositions and only recomputes when a specified key actually changes — the same tool used for state, applied here to avoid redoing work rather than to hold a mutable value. The debugging signal to watch for: a composable that feels sluggish specifically while typing or scrolling, but fine on first render, almost always has unmemoized work in its body.

Compose's core idea — describe UI as a function of state, let the framework diff and re-render only what changed — isn't Android-specific; it's the same underlying model as React on the web and SwiftUI on iOS, arriving at similar APIs (state hooks, effect scoping, component composition) independently because the same problem (keeping a UI in sync with changing data without manual bookkeeping) has converged on a similar shape of solution across the industry.

Recognizing this pattern matters practically: skills transfer. `LaunchedEffect`'s "run when this key changes, clean up when it doesn't matter anymore" is the same shape as React's `useEffect` dependency array; state hoisting is the same idea as "lifting state up" in React's own documentation. If you already think in one declarative UI framework, the mental model ports directly — what changes between frameworks is mostly syntax and a handful of framework-specific gotchas (Compose's smart recomposition granularity, React's reconciliation), not the underlying philosophy.

This topic covers Compose's concrete API; the cross-platform declarative-UI framing itself — why this pattern won across the industry — lives in the Cross-Platform group.
